question: Does intermittent fasting extend lifespan in model organisms?

starFinding.text: Yes — intermittent fasting extends lifespan in model organisms, extending rodent lifespan by up to 30% independent of total food intake and weight loss, which shows the temporal pattern of feeding rather than caloric reduction drives the benefit.
starFinding.sourceQuote: In rodents, both fasting for 24 hr every other day or twice weekly extends lifespan up to 30%, independent of both total food intake and weight loss.

top3.text: A controlled study in C. elegans measured intermittent fasting extending mean worm lifespan by 28%, the most precise single quantitative estimate in the review.
top3.sourceQuote: CR and IF extend the mean lifespan of worms by 40% and 28%, respectively.

top3.text: Across invertebrate model organisms such as worms and flies, intermittent fasting extends lifespan by 20-40%, showing the effect holds across evolutionarily divergent species.
top3.sourceQuote: In organisms such as worms and flies, intermittent fasting has been shown to extend lifespan by 20-40%.

top3.text: A defined intermittent-fasting regimen effectively extends the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans, providing direct experimental evidence in a primary study.
top3.sourceQuote: Here we establish an IF regimen that effectively extends the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans

doNotPromote: Lin et al. 2002 — 'Calorie restriction (CR) extends lifespan in a wide spectrum of organisms and is the only regimen known to lengthen the lifespan of mammals.' This is a caloric-restriction (not intermittent-fasting) result in yeast and is off-target for the IF question; it must not be ranked #1.

Fontana 2017 — the claim that CR effects 'may be due, at least in part, to intermittent fasting or daily time-restricted feeding' is a hedged background caveat about reinterpreting CR, not a direct measurement of IF extending lifespan.

Anton & Leeuwenburgh 2013 — 'intermittent fasting regimens can trigger similar biological pathways as caloric restriction, which may lead to beneficial effects on longevity' is a mechanism-analogy claim with a 'may lead to' hedge, weaker than the direct quantified lifespan findings.
